papers.title_in_file: Gaussian Process Model Kernels for Noisy Optimization in Variational Quantum Algorithms
papers.version_note: arXiv:2412.13271v1 [quant-ph], 17 Dec 2024. The text is the paper its record names.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that introduces trigonometric kernels for Gaussian process models of variational quantum algorithm cost functions and benchmarks them against standard kernels on LiH (UCCSD) and unweighted MaxCut (QAOA), including inside a GPM-enhanced line-search optimizer called RotoGP.

existing.note: The stored value is right. The paper adds that in Fig. 2(f) all kernels give particularly bad scores, and attributes this to strongly non-Gaussian shot noise for the unweighted MaxCut cost function close to the global minimum.
existing.value: The authors state that the relative gains of trigonometric kernels appear problem-dependent. They report one exception, Fig. 2(f), where the non-stationary trigonometric kernel performs worse than all the other kernels. They note that in this case all kernels give particularly bad scores, especially for a larger number of samples, and attribute it to strongly non-Gaussian shot noise for the unweighted MaxCut cost function close to the global minimum.
quotes: Additionally, the relative gains of trigonometric kernels appear problem-dependent.
An exception to this conclusion is Fig. 2(f), where the non-stationary trigonometric kernel is performing worse than all the other ones

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark uses the ground state search of the LiH molecule with one layer of UCCSD Ansatz, and the unweighted MaxCut problem on 3-regular graphs with 8 vertices solved with QAOA with 4 layers. Both problems require N = 8 circuit parameters, and s = 20 shots estimate the expectation value of each observable. The simulations use the Qiskit and Qiskit-Nature packages.
quotes: The first concerns the ground state search of the LiH molecule using one layer of UCCSD Ansatz [1, 3, 6]

the second is the unweighted MaxCut combinatorial optimization problem [26] on 3-regular graphs with 8 vertices, whose solution is sought using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) with 4 layers [27].
Both problems require N = 8 circuit parameters, and we use s = 20 shots to estimate the expectation value of each observable
We performed the simulations using the Qiskit and Qiskit-Nature packages [32, 33].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own benchmark setup, Section 2.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The results are for small simulated problems (8 parameters); no hardware run is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that three sampling distributions feed the GPM: samples around the line parallel to the 5th coordinate through the global minimum, samples around the plane spanned by the 4th and 5th coordinates through the global minimum (both with distances uniformly distributed in the range [0, 0.05π]), and samples uniformly distributed in an 8D hyperball centered at the global minimum with radius r = 0.15π. They describe the hyperball case as mimicking the later stages of a local optimization.
quotes: samples randomly distributed around the line parallel to the 5th coordinate (corresponding to a parameter in the middle of the circuit) and passing through the global minimum θmin
with distances from the line uniformly distributed in the range [0, 0.05π];
samples randomly distributed around the plane spanned by the 4th and 5th coordinates and passing through θmin
with distances from the plane uniformly distributed in the range [0, 0.05π];
samples uniformly distributed in a 8D hyperball centered at θmin with radius r = 0.15π.
The latter scenario mimics the later stages of a local optimization, where the optimization algorithm is probing points in the vicinity of the true minimum.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own sampling setup, Section 2.1.
assertions.reader_inference: All three training distributions are centered on the true global minimum, so the minimum-location and minimum-value scores are measured in a favorable neighborhood.

assertions.value: The authors state that for each sampling strategy and training set size they build one hundred random training sets, with each MaxCut training set taken from a different graph. Each GPM is trained by maximizing the likelihood on the training data, and the reported score is the median over the training sets.

assertions.value: The authors state that the LiH problem is very well described by only the first two frequencies with a period of p = 2π along every coordinate line, and that the unweighted MaxCut problem is well approximated by the lowest four (the lowest) frequencies along odd (even) coordinates with a period p = π. They set the trigonometric kernel thresholds to nf = 2 for the chemistry problem, and nf = 4 (nf = 1) for odd (even) coordinate lines for combinatorial optimization.
quotes: The LiH problem is very well described by only the first two frequencies and a period of p = 2π, along every coordinate line
the unweighted MaxCut problem is instead well approximated by the lowest four (the lowest) frequencies along odd (even) coordinates, with a period p = π.

We therefore set frequency thresholds nf = 2 for trigonometric kernels along all directions for the chemistry problem, and nf = 4 (nf = 1) for odd (even) coordinate lines for combinatorial optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own kernel settings, Section 2.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The thresholds come from the Fourier analysis of the same cost functions (Appendix D), so the trigonometric kernels are given structure that was measured on the test problems; a new problem would need that spectrum first.

assertions.value: The authors define the non-stationary trigonometric kernel (nsTRIG) from a trigonometric basis with a Gaussian prior on the coefficients. They assume no correlations between weights (off-diagonal elements of the prior covariance set to zero) and set the prior variance to zero for all frequencies above the threshold nf. The kernel is described overall by 2nf + 1 hyperparameters.

We therefore set [Σp]ii = 0 for all the frequencies ni > nf , with nf the threshold frequency

assertions.value: The authors construct a kernel for an N dimensional space as an amplitude times a product of one-dimensional line kernels, one per parameter, each with its own hyperparameters. They justify this because a product of valid kernels is also a valid kernel, and the amplitude A controls the variance of the prior probability distribution at each point.
quotes: since a product of valid kernels is also a valid kernel [23]
A is an additional hyperparameter that controls the variance of the prior probability distribution at each point

assertions.value: The authors state that they add the observed variances to the diagonal of the training covariance matrix, assuming that the measurement noise is additive and follows an independent Gaussian distribution with zero mean, and that they set the prior mean to zero, which they say is common in GPM literature and fits the VQA case because a Pauli string has expectation value zero for an a-priori unknown state.
quotes: we add the observed variances in the diagonal of the training covariance matrix
we assume that the measurement noise is additive and follows an independent, Gaussian distribution with zero mean.
Moreover, in the case of VQA, the typical cost function is a weighted sum of Pauli strings, each of which has expectation value zero for an a-priori unknown state.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of the noise model its GPM assumes, Section 1.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper later shows this Gaussian assumption failing for MaxCut near the minimum (Section 2.3).

assertions.value: The authors define the minimum-location score as the distance between the location of the exact minimum and the GPM-predicted minimum location within a subspace S. The minimum search over the GPM is done by starting from a neighborhood of the global minimum point to avoid possible local minima far away from it.
quotes: We, therefore, define a first figure of merit as the distance between the location of the exact minimum and the GPMpredicted minimum location, within S,
The minimum search over the GPM-predicted manifold is done by starting from a neighborhood of the global minimum point to avoid possible local minima far away from it.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of its score and its search procedure, Section 2.2.
assertions.reader_inference: Starting the GPM minimum search near the true minimum means the metric does not test whether the GPM finds the global minimum from an arbitrary start.

assertions.value: The authors define the likelihood at the minimum, Lmin, as the likelihood that the GPM predicts the exact global minimum value at the global minimum point. They state that a prediction close to the true value but with a very small standard deviation that does not reach the true function value yields a very small likelihood. They also define a second score, δmin, from the difference between the GPM-predicted and true cost function values at the global minimum, with the cost function maximum within subspace S entering the definition.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the unweighted MaxCut problem the likelihood at the minimum first increases and then drops again for larger training set size, for all kernels, as seen in Fig. 4(b) for training data in a hyperball centered at the global minimum. They state that the results for δmin,8D exhibit similar issues, as curves stay constant or increase for large NT, and that this result is not shown.

it starts to drop again for larger NT

assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper calls the behavior counter-intuitive because model quality is expected to increase monotonically with the number of samples.

assertions.value: The authors report that along a random line through the global minimum, with the closest 80 samples out of a total of 2748 points shown, the surrogate fit significantly underestimates the true cost function values, especially at the global minimum. They state that this appears to be caused by data points close to the minimum with very low values and very small error bars that do not include the exact cost function value.
quotes: The orange dots are the closest 80 samples to this line out of a total of 2748 points.
We immediately see that the fit significantly underestimates the true cost function values, especially at the global minimum (α = 0).
This behavior appears to be caused by data points occurring close to the minimum, which have very low values and very small error bars that do not include the exact cost function value.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study, shown with one individual fit.
assertions.reader_inference: The failure rests on an individual fit and an explanation; the paper does not report how often it occurs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the anomalous points result from a breakdown of the Gaussianity assumption: with s = 20 shots, projective measurements can return almost always the lowest value in the distribution, giving a mean lower than the true one and a very small variance, so the GPM forces the fit through or near this point. They state the problem worsens with increasing training set size, since the probability of getting at least one problematic sample increases.
quotes: Such anomalous points result from a breakdown of the Gaussianity assumption on the data.

It can happen that, taking s = 20 shots, projective measurements return almost always the lowest value in the distribution, leading to a mean lower than the true one and, crucially, to a very small variance.
This problem worsens with increasing training set size (but keeping s = 20 shots) since the probability of getting at least one of these problematic samples increases.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical explanation from one simulation study, supported by the artificial-Gaussian test.
assertions.reader_inference: The failure depends on the small shot count (s = 20); the paper does not test larger shot counts for MaxCut.

assertions.value: The authors report that when they replaced the projective measurement noise by Gaussian noise of the same mean and standard deviation, using the same number of shots, and repeated the inference on the same data, the likelihood of the minimum increased monotonically with the number of training samples (Fig. 4(e)). They also report no more isolated points with tiny error bars, and a much more reliable fit.
quotes: we repeated the same inference in a setting where we made projective measurement noise to be Gaussian by hand
obtaining that the likelihood of the minimum increases monotonically with increasing number of samples in the training set, as shown in Fig. 4(e).
As expected, there are no more isolated points with tiny error bars, and the fit is much more reliable.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the paper's test that non-Gaussian, discrete shot noise causes the MaxCut failure.

assertions.value: The authors state that the non-Gaussian shot noise issue specifically concerns cost functions made of single Pauli strings. They state that when the cost function contains multiple non-commuting observables, as in quantum chemistry and quantum many-body ground state search, the projective measurement distribution is much more similar to a Gaussian and much less skewed.
quotes: We remark that the previous issue specifically concerns cost functions made of single Pauli strings
when the cost function contains multiple non-commuting observables, like in quantum chemistry and quantum many-body ground state search
the projective measurement distribution for the cost function is much more similar to that of Gaussian and much less skewed.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement; the paper reports no separate test of it.
assertions.reader_inference: The LiH results in the paper are consistent with this, but the paper does not test the claim directly.

assertions.value: The authors report that the test likelihood monotonically increases with training set size, and that in both problems the trigonometric kernels provide a better overall cost function fit than the other kernels. They state this is especially true for the LiH ground state search, where they observe much larger test likelihoods than for the unweighted MaxCut problem.
quotes: Fig. 5 shows how the test likelihood monotonically increases for increasing training set size NT
In both problems, the trigonometric kernels provide a better overall cost function fit than the other kernels.
This is especially true for the LiH ground state search (top row), where we observe much larger test likelihoods than for the unweighted MaxCut problem (bottom row).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors define RotoGP as the combination of the RotoSolve optimizer with a GPM. Its strategy is to update one parameter per iteration while keeping all the others fixed. A good surrogate model can use information from all samples in the training set, including samples not located on the current coordinate line.
quotes: In particular, we combine the RotoSolve optimizer introduced in Ref. [31] with a GPM and call this new optimizer RotoGP.
Its strategy is to update one parameter per iteration while keeping all the others fixed.
in principle using information from all samples in the training set, also samples that are not locatd on the current coordinate line
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of its optimizer, Section 3.

For the quantum chemistry problem the optimization starts from a random point in parameter space rather than from all parameters at zero.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the RotoGP optimization the periodic squared-exponential (pSE) kernel also improves on the case without GPM, but by less than the trigonometric kernels, and that all the other kernels give results similar to the case without GPM. In the conclusions they state that other standard kernels performed significantly worse or, in some cases, even failed to improve over the base RotoSolve algorithm.
quotes: This is also true for the pSE kernel, but the improvement is smaller than the one corresponding to the trigonometric kernels.
On the other hand, all the other kernels provide similar results to the case without GPM, proving that a good choice of the kernel is crucial.
whereas other standard kernels performed significantly worse or, in some cases, even failed to improve over the base RotoSolve algorithm.

assertions.reader_inference: Section 3 says the other kernels are similar to no GPM, while Section 4 says significantly worse in some cases; the two statements differ in strength.

assertions.value: The authors state that overall they observe that the trigonometric kernels show the best performance in most of the cases under study, and that trigonometric kernels demonstrate superior GPM fitting performance on static benchmarks such as the distance-to-minimum.

assertions.value: The authors state that very little attention has been given to which kernel choices are best suited for tackling VQA problems, and that they introduce trigonometric kernels as a novel class of kernels tailored for periodic VQA cost functions.
quotes: Despite its importance, very little attention has been given to which kernel choices are best suited for tackling VQA problems.
We have introduced trigonometric kernels, a novel class of kernels tailored for periodic VQA cost functions.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about the state of the literature, with no survey in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the advantages of trigonometric kernels are most apparent when only very few and noisy samples are available, and that this makes them particularly suitable for quantum hardware where measurements are costly, such as Rydberg atom and ion-trap platforms, as opposed to faster superconducting hardware.
quotes: The advantages of trigonometric kernels are most apparent when only very few and noisy samples are available.
This makes them particularly suitable for quantum hardware where measurements are costly, such as Rydberg atom and ion-trap platforms, as opposed to faster superconducting hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper reports only simulations and no hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that trigonometric kernels are able to utilize data from the entire parameter space rather than relying on nearby points, which could explain their strong performance, and that this property suggests they may especially excel in global optimization algorithms.
quotes: from the entire parameter space rather than relying on nearby points, which could explain their strong performance.
This property suggests they may especially excel in global optimization algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conjecture; the paper does not test global optimizers.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper tests only local line-search optimization (RotoGP) and subspace fits, not global optimizers.

assertions.value: The authors state that in few-shot limits care must be taken regarding the distribution of the shot noise, which might not be Gaussian but rather follow a generalized Bernoulli distribution, as encountered for the MaxCut QAOA problem. They state that adapting the GPM framework to correctly incorporate such distributions could be an interesting future research direction.
quotes: However, in such few-shots limits, care must be taken regarding the distribution of the shot noise, which might not be Gaussian but rather follow a generalized Bernoulli distribution [2], as we have encountered for the case of the MaxCut QAOA problem.
Adapting the GPM framework to correctly incorporate such distributions could be an interesting future research direction.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit and open problem itself, Section 4, backed by its Section 2.3 MaxCut analysis.
assertions.reader_inference: The limit applies in the few-shot regime that the authors also name as where the kernels help most.

assertions.value: The authors state that this work invites future research to identify broader classes of optimization algorithms and VQA problems suited to particular kernels.
quotes: Overall, this invites future research to identify broader classes of optimization algorithms and VQA problems suited to particular kernels.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this open problem itself, Section 4.
